pages.title: Start here: how this workspace runs

text.text: A ten-minute tour of how the company's work flows through this workspace. Share it with the office manager, the estimator and every electrician.
What lives where
Customers
: homeowners, builders, landlords and businesses, with their service size and building age, what they owe, and how many jobs are open.
Jobs
: every estimate and job, with the lead electrician, date, price, materials and labor cost, and margin.
Permits and inspections
: each permit, its status, the inspection date, and the inspector's notes.
Materials
: wire, devices, breakers and panels on the trucks and shelves, and what needs ordering.
Invoices
: deposits, progress bills and final bills: sent, paid and late.
A job from first call to paid
The estimator walks the job and adds it as
New request
with the quote and costs.
When the customer says yes, set the date and lead electrician and move it to
Scheduled
. An electrician can press
Assign to me
to take it.
If it needs a permit, add one in Permits and inspections and file it before work starts.
Rough-in, inspection, finish, final inspection. Update the permit each step.
Mark done
after the final passes; it stamps the date.
Send the invoice. Past due becomes
Overdue
; the customer's Awaiting payment counts sent and overdue together.
Mark paid
stamps the payment date.
Your rhythm
Every morning: Dashboard, overdue jobs, inspections this week, corrections
Every Monday: inspections in the next 7 days, confirm with the customer that someone will be home
Every Friday: truck and shelf count in Materials
Every month: thin margins and callbacks with the team
Making it yours

Rename work types and permit kinds to match your city, add your suppliers, and delete the sample customers once you have entered a dozen of your own. Type in any cell or drag cards between columns; every total updates by itself.
Jobs by status, revenue by type of work and unpaid invoices.
Overdue jobs
My jobs
Overdue invoices
Awaiting payment (sent and overdue)
Inspections this week
Corrections to fix
An estimate is a promise. Price it from what you saw in the building, not what you hope is behind the drywall, and write down what is not included.
Walk the job first
Look up the customer.
Service size
and
Building built (year)
tell you a lot before you arrive: a 1940s house on 60 amps will need more than the customer thinks.
Open the panel. Note make, condition, available spaces, double taps, aluminum branch wiring, and signs of heat.
Measure the runs. For an EV charger or hot tub, measure panel to load, count the walls and floors you go through, and note whether the run is finished or open.
Do the load math for anything big. If the new load does not fit, the estimate includes a service upgrade or a load management device, and you explain why.
Take photos of the panel, the meter and every wall you will open.
Build the price
Materials
: from the Materials list at your real cost, plus your markup.
Labor
: hours for each person, apprentice and journeyman priced separately.
Permit and inspection
fees, and a trip for every inspection.
Patch and paint
: say whether you do it or the customer does. This is where most disputes start.
Contingency
on old houses: plaster, hidden splices, ungrounded circuits.
Enter the quote, materials cost, labor cost and hours on the job. The
Margin
column shows what you will keep; under twenty percent shows as Thin and should be repriced before it goes out.
What to write on every estimate
Scope in plain words: what you will install, where, and to what code
What is not included: drywall finishing, utility fees, trenching, furniture moving
How long the power will be off, and on which day
Permit and inspection dates as best you know them
Payment terms: deposit, progress payment, balance on final inspection
Example

A homeowner wants a 48-amp charger in a detached garage. The house has a 150 A panel with three spaces and gas heat. The load calculation leaves room for a 60 A circuit. The run is 70 feet, half of it buried. The estimator prices wire, conduit, a trench, the charger circuit, the permit and two inspections; labor is six hours for a journeyman and apprentice. The quote goes out with the trench restoration listed as not included, and the customer approves the same day.
After the job
Compare actual parts and hours with the estimate. If a kind of job keeps coming in over, change your price for it, not just the next quote.
Work that fails inspection costs twice. Work done without a permit can cost the customer their insurance claim. Treat the permit as part of the job, not paperwork after it.
When you need a permit

Most places require one for new circuits, panel and service changes, EV chargers, generators, hot tubs, and any rewiring. Small like-for-like swaps (a switch, an outlet, a light fixture on an existing box) usually do not. When in doubt, call the permit office and write down who you spoke to.
Filing
Add the permit in
Permits and inspections
, link it to the job, and set status
To file
File it, enter the number and
Filed on
, and set status
Filed
When it is issued, set
Issued
and book the first inspection date. The inspection calendar and the Next 7 days list show what is coming.
Post the permit card on site where the inspector can see it.
Before the rough-in inspection
Boxes secured, at the right height, with room for devices
Cables stapled within 12 inches of boxes and every 4.5 feet
Nail plates where cable passes within 1 1/4 inches of a stud face
Grounds made up in every box
Panel labeled with the new circuits
Drywall stays off until the inspection passes
Before the final
Every device and cover plate on, every circuit labeled
GFCI and AFCI protection tested where required
Torque on lugs and breakers checked and written down
Smoke and CO alarms working where the work triggers them
Customer walked through the panel and any new equipment
When it fails
Set the permit to
Correction needed
and write the inspector's exact words in
Inspector notes

. Fix it within two working days, book the re-inspection, and tell the customer what changed. Corrections show on the Dashboard until they pass. If the same correction comes up twice in a quarter, it is a training topic for the next team meeting.
Example

A restaurant's kitchen circuits fail the final: the walk-in cooler needs a disconnect within sight of the unit. Casimir adds the disconnect the next morning, the office books the re-inspection, and the permit moves to Final passed two days later. The job is then marked done and the balance invoice goes out.
Every electrician knows the rules. Accidents happen when someone is rushed, tired, or sure the circuit is dead. This page is the habit we keep on every job, no matter how small.
Before you touch anything
Identify every source: the panel, a sub-panel, a generator, solar, a UPS in an office.
Turn it off and lock it out with your own lock and tag. One person, one lock. Nobody removes another person's lock.
Test your meter on a known live source, test the circuit, then test the meter again (live-dead-live).
Treat neutrals as live until proven otherwise, especially on shared neutrals in older homes.
Daily checklist
Meter, leads and non-contact tester checked
Gloves and eye protection rated for the work
Ladders inspected, fiberglass only near electrical work
Lock and tag kit on the truck
Fire extinguisher and first aid kit on the truck
Customer told which rooms will lose power and for how long
Working live

Live work is the exception, never the plan. If a job truly needs it (troubleshooting with a meter, for example), the lead electrician decides, uses the right PPE for the energy level, and keeps a second person nearby.
Apprentices

An apprentice never works alone on a panel or service. The journeyman checks every termination before covers go back on, and explains why. Short daily lessons on site are how the next journeyman is made.
Old houses

Expect anything in buildings older than about 1970: knob-and-tube spliced to modern cable, ungrounded outlets that look grounded, and aluminum branch wiring. Mark what you find on the customer's record so the next person is not surprised.
If something goes wrong
Make the area safe. Do not touch a person in contact with a live conductor; cut the power first.
Call emergency services for any shock with symptoms, burns or a fall.
Call the owner, then write down what happened the same day, with photos.
Review it at the next team meeting: what made it possible, and what we change.
Example

On a troubleshooting call in a 1950s duplex, Faye locks out the breaker for the kitchen circuit and tests: the outlet is still live. A second circuit shares the box. She finds it, locks it out too, and notes the shared box on the customer's record before closing up.
